function.name: cmd_controller_execute
function.description: Executes a system-level command using os.system() on Windows operating systems. It can execute single or multiple commands chained with '&&'. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

command.description: The system command to be executed. To execute multiple commands, separate them with '&&'. For example, 'dir && echo done'.

unit.description: Specifies the unit of measure for the command if applicable. This is not utilized by os.system() directly but can be used for logging or analysis purposes.

message.content:
Below you’ll find a quick‑start guide that lets you **detect whether any VPN client is currently installed** on your Windows PC – from the most common commercial solutions down to the native “built‑in” VPN support that ships with Windows 10/11.

> ⚠️ *If you’re running this on a corporate device, make sure you have permission before executing any scripts.*

---

## 1️⃣ Quick manual checks

| What to look at | How |
|-----------------|-----|
| **Control Panel → Programs & Features** | Search for words such as “VPN”, “AnyConnect”, “OpenVPN”, “NordVPN”, “ExpressVPN”, “Cisco Secure Client”, etc. |
| **Start Menu shortcuts** | Look for icons named after popular VPN services. |
| **Taskbar/System tray** | Hover over each icon; many VPN clients leave a small icon there when active. |

These methods work well if you only need a one‑off confirmation.

---

## 2️⃣ Automated discovery with PowerShell

### 2.1 List all installed packages that contain “VPN”

```powershell
$searchTerm = '*VPN*'
Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*, `
                  HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* |
    Select-Object DisplayName, InstallDate |
    Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -like $searchTerm }
```

This pulls entries from both the **machine‑wide** (`HKLM`) and **current‑user** (`HKCU`) uninstall registries—where most installers write their metadata.

#### Example output

```
DisplayName          InstallDate
-----------          ----------
NordVPN              12/01/2025
Cisco AnyConnect     03/15/2024
...
```

### 2.2 Query WMI/CIM for more detailed info

```powershell
Get-CimInstance -Namespace root/cimv2 -ClassName Win32_Product |
Where-Object { $_.Name -match '(?i)(anyconnect|openvpn|expressvpn|nordvpn)' } |
Select-Object Name, Vendor, Version, InstallLocation
```

> 💡 Some modern installers (e.g., Microsoft Store apps) don’t register themselves under `Win32_Product`. In those cases, the above method won’t catch them.

### 2.3 Detect the built‑in Windows VPN client

Windows includes its own VPN stack (PPTP/L2TP/IPSec/etc.). You can see what connections exist:

```powershell
Get-VpnConnection
```

If nothing shows up, then either no custom VPN profiles were created or none are present.

---

## 3️⃣ One‑liner for the terminal (via CMD)

If you prefer staying inside a classic Command Prompt window, here’s a compact way to pull similar data:

```batch
@echo off
for /f "tokens=*" %%A in ('reg query HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall ^| findstr /I "VPN"') do (
   reg query "%%~A" /ve /t REG_SZ /d DisplayName >nul 2>&1 &&
   echo Installed VPN found: %%~A
)
pause
```

Save the snippet as `check_vpns.bat`, double‑click it, and watch the console report any matches.

---

## 4️⃣ Common VPN clients to look for

| Brand | Typical installation folder | Registry key hint |
|-------|-----------------------------|-------------------|
| **Cisco AnyConnect** | `%ProgramFiles%\Cisco\Cisco AnyConnect Secure Mobility Client` | `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Cisco Systems\SecureClient` |
| **OpenVPN GUI** | `%AppData%\OpenVPN` | `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\OpenVPN Technologies\OpenVPN-GUI` |
| **NordVPN** | `%LocalAppData%\NordVPN` | `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\nordvpn.com` |
| **ExpressVPN** | `%ProgramFiles%\ExpressVPN` | `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Wow6432node\ExpressVPN` |
| **Tunnelblick** *(macOS)* | N/A | — |
| **ProtonVPN** | `%ProgramFiles%\ProtonVPN` | `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Proton Technologies Ltd.` |

Feel free to add other vendor strings relevant to your environment.

---

## 5️⃣ Wrap‑up checklist

1. Run the PowerShell script(s) above to enumerate potential VPN installations.
2. Verify against the list of known vendors.
3. If you discover a VPN profile but aren’t sure who owns it, inspect the properties:
   ```powershell
   Get-VpnConnection <ProfileName>
   ```
4. Document findings in whatever asset inventory or compliance log you maintain.

That’s it! With these few lines of code—or even a quick manual scan—you’ll always know whether a VPN solution sits on your workstation. Happy hunting!
